lesson.title: Branching Out: Multiplying Along the Path
lesson.summary: A tree diagram turns a multi stage random process into labeled branches, where multiplying along a path gives a joint probability and adding across paths gives a total probability.
lesson.body:
A tree diagram is a picture of a random process that unfolds in stages. The first set of branches, coming out of a single starting point, represents the possible outcomes of stage one, each labeled with its probability. From the end of each of those branches, a new set of branches represents the possible outcomes of stage two, but now the labels are conditional probabilities, the chance of each stage two outcome given that you arrived via that particular stage one branch. At every fork, the probabilities on the branches leaving that fork must add up to 1, because together they cover every possibility from that point.

The payoff of drawing the tree is that it turns the general multiplication rule into a simple visual rule: multiply the probabilities along any complete path from start to end to get the probability of that whole sequence happening, P(A and B) equals P(A) times P(B given A). If an outcome can be reached by more than one path through the tree, add up the probabilities of all the paths that lead to it, since those paths are mutually exclusive ways of reaching the same result.

Here is a worked example. A factory has two machines. Machine A produces 60 percent of all items, and machine B produces the other 40 percent, so the first set of branches is labeled 0.6 and 0.4. Machine A's items are defective 3 percent of the time, so from the machine A branch, the next branches are labeled 0.03 for defective and 0.97 for not defective. Machine B's items are defective 5 percent of the time, so from the machine B branch, the next branches are labeled 0.05 for defective and 0.95 for not defective.

There are four complete paths through this tree. Multiply along each one: machine A and defective is 0.6 times 0.03, which is 0.018. Machine A and not defective is 0.6 times 0.97, which is 0.582. Machine B and defective is 0.4 times 0.05, which is 0.020. Machine B and not defective is 0.4 times 0.95, which is 0.380. As a check, all four paths should account for every item, so they should sum to 1: 0.018 plus 0.582 plus 0.020 plus 0.380 equals exactly 1.000, confirming the tree is built correctly.

To find the overall probability that a randomly chosen item is defective, add up every path that ends in "defective," since an item can be defective whether it came from machine A or machine B: 0.018 plus 0.020 equals 0.038, so 3.8 percent of all items are defective. That single number, 0.038, came from combining two different multiplication rule calculations, which is exactly what a tree diagram is built to organize.
